paper.title: An Investigation of The Effect of Block-Based Programming and Unplugged Coding Activities on Fifth Graders’ Computational Thinking Skills, Self-Efficacy and Academic Performance
paper.abstract: This paper investigated the effect of block-based programming and unplugged coding teaching activities on fifth graders’ computational thinking skills, self-efficacy, and academic performance. The teaching activities were conducted within the scope of the “Problem-Solving and Programming” unit of the Information Technologies and Software (ITS) course. The sample consisted of 82 fifth graders of three public middle schools in the academic year of 2020-2021. Participants were recruited using random sampling. The study adopted an embedded mixed design. The quantitative stage employed a pretest-posttest randomized control group design, while the qualitative staged employed a case study. Quantitative data were collected using the Computational Thinking Self-efficacy Scale (CTSES), the International Informatics and Computational Thinking Activity Task Test (IICTATT), and a Computational Thinking Performance Test (CTPT) developed by the researcher. Qualitative data were collected using a semi-structured interview questionnaire. The quantitative data were analyzed using the Kruskal Wallis H, paired sample t-test, and ANCOVA test on the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS). The qualitative data were analyzed inductively using MAXQDA. There was no significant difference in CTSES scores between groups. Experimental 2 had higher IICTATT and CTPT scores than Experimental-1 and control groups. The qualitative findings were grouped into seven categories.

paper.title: Effects of Scratch-based activities on 4th-grade students’ computational thinking skills
paper.abstract: Computational Thinking (CT) has emerged in recent years as a thematic trend in education in many countries. initiatives have been developed for its inclusion in school curricula. There are many pedagogical strategies to promote the development of elementary school students’ CT skills and knowledge. Unplugged learning tasks, block-based programming projects, and educational robotics are 3 of the most used strategies. This paper aimed to analyze the effect of Scratch-based activities, developed during one scholar year, on the computational thinking skills developed and concepts achieved by 4th-grade students. The study involved 189 students from two school clusters organized into an experimental group and a control group. To assess students’ computational knowledge, the Beginners Computational Thinking Test developed by Several Zapata-Cáceres et al. (2020) was used. The results indicate statistically significant differences between the groups, in which students in the experimental group (who performed activities with scratch) scored higher on the test than students in the control group (who did not use Scratch).

paper.title: Coding Science: The Role of Block-Based Programming Activities in Enhancing Computational Thinking and Science Achievement
paper.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper.abstract: In the digital era, fostering computational thinking (CT) skills is essential for scientific literacy and engaging students in authentic scientific practices. Block-based programming environments (BBPEs), such as Scratch, effectively integrate these skills into K-12 science by lowering the syntax barrier, allowing a focus on scientific logic. This study investigated the impact of a Scratch-integrated science intervention on sixth-grade students’ CT and science achievement using a quasi-experimental design. Participants ( n = 51) were assigned to either an experimental group receiving BBPEs or a control group following the standard curriculum. To ensure methodological rigor, CT test was first adapted and validated for the Turkish context ( n = 353). Despite the benefits of BBPEs, implementation poses unique challenges for science teachers, necessitating new technical and pedagogical demands. Therefore, this research supported the quantitative data with the lived experiences of the teacher who underwent this integration process. Quantitative results indicate that the intervention significantly enhanced students’ CT ( p < .05). While both groups showed gains in science achievement, the experimental group achieved higher mean scores, though the difference was not statistically significant. Qualitative findings revealed that the instructor successfully navigated the liminal space of teacher re-novicing, fostering a collaborative environment that empowered lower-achieving students to emerge as programming experts. Furthermore, the integration promoted epistemic synergy and an iterative debugging mindset, transforming experimental failures into productive inquiry steps that strengthened student persistence and understanding. This research provides empirical evidence for using BBPEs to bridge computer science and science education while highlighting the support needed for teachers during this transition.

paper.title: Enhancing computational thinking through coding education in primary school students: an experimental study on the impact of early programming exposure on problem-solving skills
paper.abstract: Introduction This research paper presents an empirical investigation of the effectiveness of early coding instruction in improving problem-solving skills and computational thinking (CT) among primary school students. The primary research question was to determine whether a structured six-month coding intervention yields greater cognitive gains in children aged 8–12 than instruction without coding. Methods The study employed a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with 200 students randomly assigned to an experimental group ( n = 100) and a control group ( n = 100). The experimental group participated in a 24-week curriculum using Scratch and Python, while the control group followed the standard school curriculum. To assess skill acquisition and practice intensity, paired-sample t -tests, independent-sample t -tests, and Pearson correlation analyses were conducted. Results The findings indicate statistically significant effects for the experimental group, with problem-solving scores increasing to 23.5 from a mean of 17.8 ( p < 0.001) and computational thinking scores increasing to 30.6 from a mean of 20.4 ( p < 0.001), reflecting large effect sizes. In contrast, the control group exhibited no significant gains. Conclusion From a theoretical perspective, the study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that the concrete operational stage of development (ages 7–11) represents a critical period for the development of abstract algorithmic thinking through programming. From a practical standpoint, the results provide evidence-based support for integrating coding into primary education not merely as a professional competency, but as a cognitive development opportunity essential for 21st-century digital literacy.

paper.title: The Effect of the Modality on Students’ Computational Thinking, Programming Attitude, and Programming Achievement
paper.venue: International Journal of Computer Science Education in Schools
paper.abstract: The purpose of the current study was to explore the effect of modality (constructionist mBlock, Scratch, and Python interventions) on six-grade students’ computational thinking, programming attitude, and achievement. The pre-test and post-test quasi-experimental design was used to explore the research questions. The study group consisted of 105 six grade students from three different classes. A constructionist learning environment was formed for Scratch, mBlock, and Python groups. All groups were given 8 week-instruction. Instruction included two forty-minute sessions each week. The data were collected through the programming achievement test, computational thinking test, and computer programming attitude scale. The results of the study showed that mBlock group outperformed the Scratch and Python groups with respect to computer programming attitude. Students who attended mBlock and Scratch groups had higher levels of programming achievement than those of the students who attended the Python group. No significant differences with respect to computational thinking were observed between the groups. This study has implications for educators who are teaching computational thinking and programming. Further research was recommended to explore the effect of modality.

paper.title: Do We Really Need Block-Based Programming to Enhance Computational Thinking in Science Classes?
paper.venue: Necatibey Eğitim Fakültesi Elektronik Fen ve Matematik Eğitimi Dergisi
paper.abstract: As a result of technological developments, digital technologies are increasing their impact in all areas of life. This impact complicates the problems that need to be solved while diversifying the ways to solve them. This research addresses the use of computational thinking, one of the diversified problem-solving approaches, in science education. In this context, the research aims to determine the effect of a block-based coding tool on the enhancement of computational thinking skills. To this objective, the study, designed with a quasi-experimental design, aims to determine the effect of block-based coding and the algorithmic explanation approach on academic achievement and computational thinking skills. In the study conducted with sixth-grade middle school students, five different computational thinking activities were carried out over sixteen class hours. The results of the study showed no significant difference in science achievement between the experimental and control groups. However, significant differences in favor of the control group were found in the overall computational thinking scale and in the cooperativity and problem solving sub-dimensions. Based on this result, it can be argued that block-based coding contributes more positively to the development of computational thinking than the algorithmic explanation approach. However, the science achievement, creativity, algorithmic thinking, and critical thinking sub-dimensions, which did not show significant differences, indicate the potential positive effect of the algorithmic explanation approach. Therefore, it can be considered an important alternative, especially in situations where a digital divide can be observed.

paper.title: The Impact of SRA-Programming on Computational Thinking in a Visual Oriented Programming Environment
paper.abstract: Abstract Visual programming environments are popular instruments in teaching Computational Thinking (CT) in schools today. Applying Sense-Reason-Act (SRA) programming can influence the development of computational thinking when forcing pupils to anticipate the unforeseen in their computer programs. SRA-programming originates from the programming of tangible robots, but can also be of equal value in visual programming with on-screen output. The underlying rationale is that programming in a visual programming environment using SRA leads to more understanding of the computational concepts addressed, resulting in a higher level of computational skill compared to visual programming without the application of SRA. Furthermore, it has been hypothesised that if pupils in a visual programming environment can anticipate unforeseen events and solve programming tasks by applying SRA, they will be better able to solve complex computational thinking tasks. To establish if characteristic differences in the development of computational thinking can be measured when SRA-programming is applied in a visual programming environment with an on-screen output, we assessed the applicability of SRA-programming with visual output as the main component of the execution of developed code. This research uses a pre-test post-test design that reveals significant differences in the development of computational thinking in two treatment conditions. To assess CT, the Computational Thinking Test (CTt) was used. Results show that when using SRA-programming in a visual programming environment it leads to an increased understanding of complex computational concepts, which results in a significant increase in the development of computational thinking.

paper.title: Effect of SRA-programming on computational thinking through different output modalities
paper.abstract: Abstract The application of sense-reason-act (SRA) programming in contemporary education can ensure the development of computational thinking (CT) at a more advanced level. SRA-programming has been identified as an instrumental way of thinking for learning to program robots and encourages the development of the more complex concepts of programming. Visual programming environments are diverse in appearance and prove to be an excellent way to teach pupils the basic ideas of programming. It is important to investigate whether the type of output has a characteristic influence on the level of development of CT in visual programming environments. In this research, we therefore explore whether characteristic differences in the development of CT can be measured when SRA-programming is applied in a visual programming environment with an on-screen output or a tangible output. It was expected that the observed effect of pupils' programming actions through the application of SRA would show that the type of output influences the understanding of complex programming concepts at a higher level. Our results indicate that SRA-programming with visual, on-screen output yields a significant increase in the development of CT, as opposed to SRA-programming with a tangible output. The development of complex programming concepts can also be demonstrated.

en.background: Fostering computational thinking skills in school education is increasingly vital for preparing young learners to solve complex problems in digital environments.
en.conclusionAbstract: Block-based programming instruction can effectively foster computational thinking across primary and lower secondary classrooms compared to both passive and active alternatives.
introduction: Computational thinking has emerged as an essential skill within primary and lower secondary school curricula. As schools aim to prepare young learners for problem-solving in modern technology-rich societies, introducing algorithmic thinking and programming principles during elementary and middle school grades has become a major educational priority. However, implementing programming instruction in early grades requires pedagogical approaches that are developmentally appropriate for novice students.

Visual and block-based programming environments, such as Scratch, allow students to assemble programs using graphical blocks rather than typing text-based code. The included primary studies evaluated various block-based implementations across elementary and middle school grades, ranging from standalone visual programming activities [S1, S3] to visual coding integrated into science curricula [S4, S7]. Other studies investigated block-based curricula that transition into text-based languages [S5] or focused on structured visual frameworks such as Sense-Reason-Act programming environments [S8, S9].

Although numerous empirical evaluations have examined visual programming, their findings are distributed across distinct instructional settings, comparison conditions, and school levels. Prior studies have compared block-based instruction to passive baselines [S1, S3, S4, S9] as well as active instructional alternatives [S2, S6, S7, S8]. A quantitative synthesis is therefore useful to combine these diverse findings into a single pooled estimate. The purpose of this meta-analysis is to evaluate the effects of block-based programming instruction on computational thinking in school students, examining overall efficacy as well as potential variations across school levels and comparison types.
discussion: The synthesis revealed a statistically significant, large overall effect of block-based programming instruction on computational thinking outcomes (g = 1.47, 95% CI [0.87, 2.06], p < .001; Table 3). Across the included studies, effect sizes consistently favored the intervention over comparison groups (Fig. 1). Substantial heterogeneity was present across the sample of studies (Q(8) = 63.62, p < .001, I2 = 87.4%, tau2 = 0.413; Table 3), accompanied by a wide prediction interval of [−0.15, 3.08]. A sensitivity analysis examining leave-one-out estimates demonstrated that the pooled effect remained relatively stable, ranging from 1.32 to 1.60.

Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore school level and comparison type, although these comparisons are exploratory and based on few studies. In the analysis by school level (Table 3), elementary samples showed a large effect (k = 6, g = 1.41, 95% CI [0.57, 2.25]), which did not differ significantly from the middle school samples (k = 3, g = 1.58, 95% CI [−0.63, 3.79]; Q(1) = 0.08, p = .783). Similarly, when examining comparison types, active comparisons yielded an estimate of g = 1.94 (95% CI [0.49, 3.39], k = 4), whereas passive comparisons yielded g = 1.14 (95% CI [0.50, 1.78], k = 5), with no statistically significant subgroup difference (Q(1) = 2.44, p = .118). Because of the small number of studies in these subsets, these subgroup differences remain exploratory and cannot establish definitive causes.

An inspection of the individual studies summarized in Table 1 and Table 2 reveals variations across instructional designs and control conditions. Large effects were reported in elementary cohorts when Scratch was contrasted with regular algorithm instruction (g = 2.67 [S2]) and when visual Sense-Reason-Act concepts were contrasted with linear visual programming (g = 2.05 [S8]). Moderate to large effects occurred in elementary evaluations comparing block-based instruction with regular curriculum controls (g = 0.92 [S1]; g = 1.16 [S3]; g = 1.60 [S5]; g = 0.41 [S9]). In middle school cohorts, block-based learning produced substantial gains over text-based Python instruction (g = 2.42 [S6]) and regular science lessons (g = 1.67 [S4]), while comparison against unplugged algorithmic instruction in science yielded a smaller effect (g = 0.65 [S7]).

For teachers of grades 1-9, these findings indicate that block-based programming environments can serve as an effective means to develop student computational thinking. Visual environments may be implemented as dedicated computing units or integrated within subject areas such as science. Furthermore, teachers working with novice learners may find visual block platforms beneficial when introducing algorithmic principles before or alongside text-based or unplugged instructional alternatives.
limitations: This meta-analysis has several limitations. The synthesis is based on a small total evidence base of 9 studies encompassing 806 participants, which restricts statistical power, prevented the assessment of publication bias, and means subgroup findings must be regarded as exploratory. Furthermore, the underlying data were extracted automatically, which may limit the precision of nuanced study characteristics.

In addition, the included studies displayed variability in study designs and assessment instruments. The evidence base comprises both randomized controlled trials [S1, S5, S8, S9] and quasi-experimental designs [S2, S3, S4, S6, S7]. Outcome measures also varied from standardized computational thinking tests to specific programming achievement tests and self-report scales, contributing to the substantial heterogeneity observed across findings.
conclusion: In conclusion, this meta-analysis of 9 studies indicates that block-based programming instruction has a large positive effect on computational thinking in school students compared to both passive and active control conditions. Although the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity require cautious interpretation, visual block-based tools provide a promising approach for cultivating algorithmic and computational skills across grades 1 through 9.

ja.background: 学校教育における計算論的思考（computational thinking）の育成は，デジタル環境で複雑な問題を解決する児童生徒を育てる上で重要性を増している．
ja.conclusionAbstract: ブロック型プログラミング指導は，受動的・能動的な対照群の双方と比較して，小・中学校の授業において計算論的思考を効果的に育成できる．
introduction: 計算論的思考は，初等・中等教育のカリキュラムにおいて不可欠な資質・能力として浮上してきた．現代の技術に富んだ社会における問題解決に向けて子どもたちを準備させることが学校に求められるなか，小学校および中学校の段階でアルゴリズム的思考やプログラミングの基本原理を導入することは，主要な教育的優先課題となっている．しかし，早期の学年におけるプログラミング指導の実践には，初心者の児童生徒の発達段階に適した指導法が必要とされる．

Scratchに代表されるビジュアルおよびブロック型のプログラミング環境は，児童生徒がテキストベースのコードを入力するのではなく，視覚的なブロックを用いてプログラムを組み立てることを可能にする．分析対象となった原著論文は，小学校および中学校の学年における多様なブロック型の実践を評価しており，それらは単独のビジュアルプログラミング活動 [S1, S3] から理科のカリキュラムに統合されたビジュアルコーディング [S4, S7] まで多岐にわたる．他の研究では，テキストベースの言語へと移行するブロック型カリキュラムを検討したもの [S5] や，感覚・推論・行動（Sense-Reason-Act）プログラミング環境のような構造化された視覚的フレームワークに着目したもの [S8, S9] もあった．

ビジュアルプログラミングを検証した実証的な評価は多数存在するものの，その知見は異なる指導環境，対照条件，学校段階に分散している．先行研究では，ブロック型指導を受動的なベースライン [S1, S3, S4, S9] だけでなく，能動的な指導代替案 [S2, S6, S7, S8] とも比較してきた．したがって，これら多様な知見を統合して単一の統合推定量を得るためには，定量的統合が有用である．本メタ分析の目的は，児童生徒における計算論的思考に対するブロック型プログラミング指導の効果を評価し，全体的な有効性とともに学校段階や対照群のタイプによる潜在的な差異を検討することである．
discussion: 統合の結果，計算論的思考のアウトカムに対するブロック型プログラミング指導の統計的に有意で大きな全体的効果が明らかになった（g = 1.47，95% CI [0.87, 2.06]，p < .001；表3）．含まれた研究全体において，効果量（effect size）は一貫して対照群よりも介入群を支持していた（図1）．研究サンプル全体で実質的な異質性（heterogeneity）が認められ（Q(8) = 63.62，p < .001，I2 = 87.4%，tau2 = 0.413；表3），[−0.15, 3.08] という広い予測区間を伴っていた．1研究除外（leave-one-out）推定量を検討した感度分析では，統合効果は1.32から1.60の範囲で比較的安定していることが示された．

これらの比較は探索的であり少数の研究に基づくものであるが，学校段階および対照群のタイプを探索するためにサブグループ分析が実施された．学校段階別の分析（表3）では，小学校のサンプルが大きな効果を示し（k = 6，g = 1.41，95% CI [0.57, 2.25]），中学校のサンプル（k = 3，g = 1.58，95% CI [−0.63, 3.79]；Q(1) = 0.08，p = .783）と有意な差は認められなかった．同様に，対照群のタイプを検討したところ，能動的対照群の推定値は g = 1.94（95% CI [0.49, 3.39]，k = 4）であったのに対し，受動的対照群は g = 1.14（95% CI [0.50, 1.78]，k = 5）であり，統計的に有意なサブグループ間の差は見られなかった（Q(1) = 2.44，p = .118）．これらのサブセットにおける研究数が少ないため，これらのサブグループ差は探索的なものにとどまり，決定的な要因を確定することはできない．

表1および表2に要約された個別研究の精査から，指導デザインおよび対照条件による差異が明らかになった．小学校のコホートでは，Scratchが通常のアルゴリズム指導と比較された場合（g = 2.67 [S2]），および感覚・推論・行動の視覚的概念が直線的なビジュアルプログラミングと比較された場合（g = 2.05 [S8]）に大きな効果が報告された．ブロック型指導を通常カリキュラムの対照群と比較した小学校の評価では，中程度から大きな効果が認められた（g = 0.92 [S1]；g = 1.16 [S3]；g = 1.60 [S5]；g = 0.41 [S9]）．中学校のコホートでは，ブロック型学習はテキストベースのPython指導（g = 2.42 [S6]）や通常の理科の授業（g = 1.67 [S4]）に対して大幅な向上をもたらした一方，理科におけるアンプラグドなアルゴリズム指導との比較ではより小さな効果にとどまった（g = 0.65 [S7]）．

小・中学校（1〜9年生）の教員にとって，これらの知見は，ブロック型プログラミング環境が児童生徒の計算論的思考を育成する効果的な手段となり得ることを示している．ビジュアル環境は，独立した情報分野の単元として実施することも，理科などの教科内に統合して実施することも可能である．さらに，初心者の学習者を指導する教員にとっては，テキストベースやアンプラグドな指導代替案の導入前またはそれと並行してアルゴリズムの原理を導入する際，視覚的なブロックプラットフォームが有用であると考えられる．
limitations: 本メタ分析にはいくつかの限界がある．本統合は，計806名の参加者を含む9件の研究という小規模なエビデンスベースに基づいており，これにより統計的検出力が制限され，公表バイアス（publication bias）の評価が妨げられたほか，サブグループ分析の知見を探索的なものとみなさざるを得ない．さらに，基礎データが自動抽出されたため，研究特性の微細なニュアンスに関する精度が制限されている可能性がある．

加えて，含まれた研究の研究デザインおよび評価尺度には多様性がみられた．エビデンスベースは，ランダム化比較試験（randomized controlled trial）[S1, S5, S8, S9] と準実験デザイン [S2, S3, S4, S6, S7] の双方で構成されている．アウトカムの測定方法も，標準化された計算論的思考テストから特定のプログラミング達成度テスト，自己報告式尺度まで多岐にわたり，このことが知見全体で観察された実質的な異質性に寄与している．
conclusion: 結論として，9件の研究を対象とした本メタ分析は，ブロック型プログラミング指導が受動的および能動的な対照条件の双方と比較して，児童生徒の計算論的思考に対して大きな正の効果を持つことを示している．研究数の少なさと実質的な異質性により慎重な解釈が求められるものの，視覚的なブロック型ツールは，小・中学校（1〜9年生）を通じてアルゴリズム的および計算論的スキルを育成するための有望なアプローチを提供する．

article.lead: 小・中学生を対象としたブロック型プログラミング指導が、計算論的思考力に与える影響を調べた9件の研究（計806名）のメタ分析結果をご紹介します。分析の結果、効果量g（平均の差を標準偏差で割った値）は1.47と大きなプラスの効果が示されました。視覚的にブロックを組み合わせる指導が、児童生徒の問題解決や論理的思考の育成に寄与する可能性が示唆されています。
article.question: 本分析の問いは「小・中学生へのブロック型プログラミング指導は、計算論的思考力の向上に効果があるのか」です。プログラミング教育が導入される中、学校現場では視覚的なブロックを用いた指導が児童生徒の思考力育成に本当に役立つのか関心が集まっています。通常授業や他の指導法と比べてどのような学習成果が得られるのかを整理することは、先生方が授業設計や教材選定を行う上で重要な手がかりとなります。
reading: 全体の統合結果では、効果量gが1.47（95%信頼区間[0.87, 2.06]）と統計的に有意な向上が示されました。研究を1つずつ除外して再計算してもgは1.32から1.60の範囲にとどまり、結果は一定の安定性を示しています。ただし、研究間のばらつき度合いを示す指標であるI2は87.4%と非常に高く、将来の同様の介入効果を予測する予測区間も[-0.15, 3.08]とマイナスを含むなど、指導環境による差が大きい点に留意が必要です。

学校段階別では、小学校（6件、g=1.41）と中学校（3件、g=1.58）の双方で効果が見られ、学校段階間の差は統計的に有意ではありませんでした（p=.783）。また、通常授業等と比較した受動的比較（5件、g=1.14）に加え、別の指導法と比較した能動的比較（4件、g=1.94）でも高い効果が見られました。ただし、これらは研究数が非常に少ない中での探索的な分析であり、確定的な結論を急ぐことはできません。
hints: 小学校・中学校ともに効果が示されており、発達段階に応じたブロック型教材の活用は、計算論的思考力の基礎固めに役立ちます。
通常授業との比較だけでなく、別の学習法との比較でも良好な結果が得られており、視覚的ブロックを用いた指導活動は有効な選択肢です。
理科など他教科との統合指導（[S4]や[S7]）や、順次処理から発展させた概念指導（[S8]）など、工夫次第で効果的な授業展開が期待できます。
cautions: 対象となった研究は9件（計806名）と少なく、データも自動抽出されたものであるため、過度に効果を強調せず慎重に受け止める必要があります。
研究間のばらつき（異質性）が大きく、予測区間（[-0.15, 3.08]）にマイナスが含まれるため、指導法や学級環境によっては効果が十分に出ない可能性もあります。
研究数が10件未満のため公表バイアスの評価が行われておらず、効果が肯定的な研究に偏っている可能性が否定できない点にご注意ください。
article.sns: 小・中学生のブロック型プログラミング指導に関するメタ分析（9件・806名）では思考力向上に大きな効果（g=1.47）が示されました。研究数が少なく慎重さは必要ですが、授業の参考となる結果です。
